title: AI Journey
subtitle: Machine learning from the ground up

sessions.title: Teaching a Machine from Examples
summary: Suppose you want a program that names a flower from its measurements. You could write rules by hand: short petals mean *setosa*, then check the width, then add an exception for the awkward cases. The list gets long quickly. Machine learning takes a different route: you show the computer flowers whose species is already known, and it works out the rules itself.
This notebook follows one complete experiment from start to finish. The code is short. The order of the steps is what you will reuse in every later session.

**New to notebooks, to Python or to AI?** Read *Before You Start* (`prelim_before_you_start.ipynb`) first. It shows how to run a notebook, how to follow the code without knowing Python, and the words this session uses. You don't need to read the code to follow this session: the text before each code cell says what it does, and the text after it reads the output.
outcomes: explain why part of the data is kept hidden until the end
say what a baseline is and why a model's score means little without one
look at a model's individual mistakes instead of only its accuracy
sections: The baseline: what does doing nothing clever score?
Which flowers does it get wrong?

pauses.section: The baseline: what does doing nothing clever score?
pauses.q: what accuracy would you be happy with for this problem? Decide before scrolling.
the model makes three mistakes on the test set. Which species do you expect it to mix up? The petal ranges in section 4 are a clue.

takeaways: **split** the data and put the test set aside
set a **baseline**
**fit** a model on the training set
**evaluate** on the test set
**read the errors**.

sessions.title: Reading a Dataset
summary: In Session 0 the dataset arrived ready to use. Real data rarely does: it has gaps, repeated rows and values that can't be true, and a model trained on it will learn from all of that without complaint. This session is about finding those problems before any model is built.

We use a made-up table of 500 students on an introductory course, with a column saying whether each one passed. The table has four problems planted in it. The same table (generated by the same function, with the same seed) is used again in Session 2, where we fix what we find here.

write each finding down as a decision about what to do next

sessions.title: Four Ways to Draw a Boundary
summary: In Session 2 a logistic regression was the last step of a pipeline, and we never asked whether it was a good choice. This session puts four common model families on the same problem and looks at what each one does with it.

Every model has a built-in preference for a certain kind of answer. Logistic regression draws a straight line. k-nearest neighbours copies the labels of nearby points. A decision tree asks a series of yes/no questions about one feature at a time. A random forest averages many such trees. These preferences are called the model's **inductive bias**, and they decide which patterns a model can find from the examples it is given.
outcomes: describe in a sentence how each of the four models makes a prediction

sections: Overfitting: a tree with no limits

pauses.q: the moons are curved. Before looking at the boundaries, which models do you expect to follow the curve and which to struggle?

sessions.title: Finding Structure Without Labels
summary: In Sessions 0 to 4 every example came with an answer: a species, a pass or fail, a diagnosis. Often the answers don't exist. You have the data and nobody has told you what is in it. **Unsupervised learning** looks for structure in data without being given a target.

This session covers the two main kinds: **clustering**, which groups similar points, and **dimensionality reduction**, which squeezes many features into a few so we can look at them. The main demonstration is k-means, the most common clustering method.
outcomes: describe how k-means places and refines its groups
explain why the scale of each feature changes the clusters, and see it happen

sessions.title: From a Linear Model to a Neural Network
summary: Sessions 0 to 5 used models from scikit-learn, and logistic regression came up more than once. A neural network is built from the same part: multiply the inputs by weights, add a bias, and pass the result through a function. The difference is that a network stacks these units in layers. This session shows what that stacking buys, using the smallest problem where it matters, and then opens up the step every earlier session hid inside `fit`: how a model's weights are actually learned.
From this session on, the course builds its networks with **PyTorch**, a widely used library for neural networks. It shows the training loop in plain code instead of hiding it.
outcomes: explain why a straight-line model can't solve XOR, and why layers need a non-linear step between them
write the loop that trains a model: compute the loss, compute its gradient, take a small step
build and train a small network in PyTorch, count its parameters and read its decision boundary
sections: A problem a straight line can't solve
Why layers need a non-linear step
Solving XOR by hand with two hidden units
How a model learns: a loss, a gradient and a small step

pauses.section: A problem a straight line can't solve
pauses.q: look at the four corners of the square. Can you draw one straight line with both 1s on one side and both 0s on the other?

pauses.section: Why layers need a non-linear step
pauses.q: does the chain of two linear layers have more power than one?

takeaways: A single unit makes a straight-line decision. Stacking units adds nothing unless an activation follows each layer.
Training is one loop: compute the loss, compute its gradient, move every weight a small step against the gradient. The learning rate sets the size of the step.
Backpropagation computes the gradient for every weight in every layer; in PyTorch that is `loss.backward()`.
Hidden layers learn new features from the inputs, and the output layer decides using those features. Counting parameters is simple arithmetic: for a dense layer, inputs × units + units.
Session 7 runs this loop on a harder problem and shows how to read the loss curves to tell whether training is going well.

sessions.title: Computer Vision: Why Images Need a Different Network
summary: In Session 6 a network took a handful of numbers as input. An image has thousands: a 28×28 picture has 784 pixel values. We could feed them to the same kind of network after flattening them into a row, but that throws away the layout, and the layout is most of what an image is. A **convolutional neural network (CNN)** keeps it.

This session compares a flattened dense network with a small CNN on handwritten digits. The comparison that matters is not their score on ordinary test digits. It is what happens when the digits are moved a few pixels.
outcomes: describe what a convolution filter does, and compute one by hand
explain why a CNN needs far fewer parameters than a dense network on the same image
read the shift test and say what the CNN's spatial design buys and what it doesn't
sections: Training both under the same conditions

pauses.q: the next cell builds a CNN with two convolution layers (16 filters, then 32, each 3×3) and a dense network that connects all 784 pixels to 128 units. Which one needs more parameters, and by roughly how much?
which network will lose more accuracy when the digits move 3 pixels, and why?

takeaways: A convolution filter is a small grid of weights slid over the whole image. It uses the same weights at every position.
That sharing makes a CNN much smaller than a dense network on the same image: 12,810 parameters against 101,770 here.
The benefit appears most clearly when the data changes in a way the architecture expects. When digits moved by 2 pixels, the CNN lost 5.9 points and the dense network 24.8.
A CNN is not shift-proof. For the remaining gap, augment the training data.
A high test score is not enough. Check how the model behaves when the input changes, and look at its mistakes.

sessions.title: Transfer Learning: Reusing a Trained Network
summary: In Session 8 we trained a CNN on 10,000 digits. Photographs are harder, and collecting millions of labelled ones is out of reach for most projects. The usual answer is to start from a network that someone else has already trained on a very large photo collection, and adapt it.

We compare three ways of getting a flower classifier from 1,400 training photos, with everything else held fixed: a network trained from scratch, a pretrained network used as a fixed feature extractor, and a pretrained network that is then fine-tuned.
outcomes: describe a network as a backbone plus a small task head, and say what "frozen" means
read a three-way comparison and say which differences are large enough to trust
explain why the held-out photos must be chosen once, by file, and not reshuffled
sections: Augmentation: extra views of the same photo
The three runs side by side

pauses.q: the next cell makes random changes to a training photo: flips it left to right, rotates it a little, zooms in or out. Which of these changes would be wrong for a dataset of handwritten digits like Session 8's?

pauses.section: The three runs side by side
pauses.q: before looking at the table, order the three strategies by test accuracy. How big do you expect the gaps to be?

takeaways: Start from a pretrained backbone when you have few labelled images. Here that was worth 14 points of accuracy.
Train the head first with the backbone frozen. Try fine-tuning next, with a small learning rate, and keep it only if validation shows a gain. Here it added about 3 points on both validation and test.
Split by file, once, and keep the held-out sets in a fixed order.
Change one thing between runs, report training time and parameter counts, and score the test set once per final model.

sessions.title: How Text Becomes Numbers
summary: Sessions 8 and 9 turned pictures into grids of numbers. Text needs a different step first: a sentence has to be cut into pieces and each piece given a number. This session builds that pipeline on 37,500 movie reviews labelled positive or negative, and compares two ways of reading them: counting words (TF-IDF with a logistic regression) and a small LSTM network that reads them in order.
The question to keep in mind is whether order matters. "Not good" and "good" share a word and mean opposite things.
outcomes: describe how text becomes tokens, then token ids, then vectors
explain what word pairs (bigrams) add to a word-count model, and read their effect in the weights
compare a word-count model with an LSTM on the same split and say honestly which wins here

pauses.q: the single-word model can only add up a weight for "not" and a weight for "good". The word-pair model also has a feature for "not good". What weight do you expect it to learn for that pair: positive, negative, or close to zero?
the next model reads each review in order, word by word, so it could in principle learn what "not" does to the words after it. On these 10,000 reviews, will it beat the word-pair model's 0.884?

takeaways: Text becomes tokens, then ids, then vectors. The ids are labels, not quantities.
Run a word-count baseline first. Here it scored 0.877 and was hard to beat.
Word pairs add a little order information: 0.884 against 0.877, and the "not good" weight shows how.
An LSTM reads in order but needs more data than 10,000 reviews to compete: it scored 0.825 and overfitted after two epochs.
Embeddings learn which words behave alike, but only for words the data covers well.
sessions.run: To run it yourself you need `numpy`, `pandas`, `matplotlib`, `scikit-learn`, `torch` and `huggingface_hub` (with `pyarrow` to read the files). The first run downloads the IMDB reviews from the Hugging Face hub (two files of 20 MB). The saved outputs came from a laptop GPU, where the notebook took two to three minutes. On a CPU, the LSTM is the slow part and may take several minutes. Your numbers may differ slightly from the ones quoted in the text.

sessions.title: Attention
summary: Read this sentence: *The robot put the battery in the device because **it** was empty.* What does "it" refer to? A person says "the battery" at once. To work that out, a model has to look back at earlier words and weigh them. An LSTM (Session 10) has to carry everything it might need through one running memory. **Attention** gives each word a direct way to look at every other word and decide how much each one matters. It is the core of the **transformer**, the architecture introduced in 2017 in the paper "Attention Is All You Need", on which BERT, the model used here, and the language models of Session 12 are built.
This session computes attention by hand on a small designed example, adds the mask used when generating text, and then looks at what real attention in a trained model does with the same sentence.
outcomes: describe attention as each token asking a question (a query) and collecting information from the tokens whose keys match it
explain the causal mask that stops a text generator reading ahead
read real attention weights from BERT and say what they do and don't show, and explain why it cuts text into subwords
sections: What a trained model actually does

pauses.q: which token should "it" pay most attention to? Look at the "it" row.

BERT, next, has 144 attention heads. We give it the sentence twice, once ending in "empty" (so "it" is the battery) and once in "broken" (so "it" is more likely the device). Will one head point from "it" to the right object in both sentences?

takeaways: Every token makes a query, a key and a value. Weights come from query–key matches, and the output is a weighted mix of values.
Attention gives each token a direct route to every other token, whatever the distance.
A causal mask stops a generator from reading ahead; an encoder doesn't need one.
In a real model, individual heads do not neatly resolve "it". Be careful when reading heatmaps as explanations.
Transformers read subword tokens: common words are one token, rare words several pieces, so no word is ever unknown.

sessions.title: Language Models in Systems: Retrieval, Abstaining and Prompt Injection
summary: Session 11 explained how a transformer reads text. This session uses one. We run a small open language model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, on the GPU and put it inside a **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** system: the system first finds the passages that are relevant to a question, then asks the model to answer from them. We build the whole loop, make it refuse when it has nothing relevant, and then attack it with a document that contains hidden instructions.
outcomes: explain that a language model predicts the next token in a loop, and describe the retrieve-then-generate loop built around it, measuring its two halves separately
make a system abstain when the retriever finds nothing relevant, and say how reliable that is
explain prompt injection from a live example, and say which defences held and which did not
sections: A retriever over eight short documents
Closing the loop: generate from what was retrieved

pauses.q: the request is "Suggest a name for a robot that sorts batteries." How sure do you expect the model to be of the first token of its answer?
a user asks a question that none of the documents covers. What should the system do?
the question is about thresholds, so the retriever will return both the real document and the forum post. Will the model follow the injected sentence?

takeaways: A language model predicts a probability for every possible next token and is run in a loop. Greedy decoding takes the likeliest token; sampling picks at random, and the temperature sets how adventurous it is. Fluency is not evidence of truth.
RAG = retrieve, then generate. Measure each half on its own: Recall@k and MRR for retrieval, faithfulness for answers.
Retrieval with a score threshold lets a system say "I have no document for this", which beats a fluent guess.

Anything the system retrieves can carry instructions. In our run a warning in the prompt failed and two plain prompts held, which is exactly the kind of inconsistency that makes prompt wording a poor defence.
Put the checks in the application, outside the model.

prelim.title: Before You Start — Notebooks and the Ideas Behind AI
summary: This course teaches machine learning by running real experiments. This notebook comes before Session 0. It is for anyone who has never opened a notebook, never trained a model, or never written Python. It assumes no background, and you don't have to write any code.

It has two parts. **Part 1** shows how a notebook works and how to follow the code in this course without knowing Python. **Part 2** explains the ideas the rest of the course builds on: what it means for a program to learn from examples, the words you will hear, and what each session is about.
outcomes: open a notebook, run its cells, and recover when a cell fails
follow a code cell from the text around it, its comments and its names, without knowing Python
say how machine learning differs from ordinary programming
use the words *example*, *feature*, *label*, *model*, *training* and *prediction*
